{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"eac472ed2c1ac0622ea7f26254dd6173e4912be2196402d01f888c9b3ad7605c","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:73","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Sharing the road safely","heading":"C — Sharing the road safely: pedestrians, bicycles, motorcycles, large trucks and buses and their No-Zones, school buses, slow-moving farm and animal-drawn vehicles, horseback riders, work zones, trains and railroad crossings, passenger vans and recreational vehicles","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Sharing the road safely: pedestrians, bicycles, motorcycles, large trucks and buses and their No-Zones, school buses, slow-moving farm and animal-drawn vehicles, horseback riders, work zones, trains and railroad crossings, passenger vans and recreational vehicles
Knowledge domain: how Tennessee drivers share the road — who counts as a pedestrian and when to yield, how to pass and turn near bicycles, why motorcycles are hard to see and need a full lane, where trucks and buses cannot see you and how long they take to stop, how to protect children at school buses, how to approach slow-moving vehicles and horses, how to drive through work zones, how to cross railroad tracks, and what makes large passenger vans and RVs different.

FACT_ID: sec16-F01 | anchor: A01
Under Tennessee law, anyone on foot or using a motorized or non-motorized wheelchair counts as a pedestrian. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-F02 | anchor: A01
Pedestrians generally have the right-of-way at all intersections, and every intersection has a crosswalk even when no lines are painted. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-F03 | anchor: A01
Whatever the right-of-way rules say, the law requires drivers to use great care and extreme caution to avoid hitting pedestrians. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-F04 | anchor: A01
Do not stop with any part of your vehicle over the crosswalk at a red light or while waiting to turn, because it forces pedestrians around your car. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-F05 | anchor: A01
In a marked school zone with its warning flashers on, you must stop for a pedestrian crossing in a marked crosswalk or at an intersection without one, and stay stopped until the pedestrian has crossed your roadway. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-F06 | anchor: A01
Always yield to a blind pedestrian carrying a white or metallic cane with a red tip or using a guide dog. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-F07 | anchor: A02
Before crossing, stop at the curb or road edge and look left, right and left again, then check over your shoulder for turning vehicles. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-F08 | anchor: A02
If the DON'T WALK signal starts flashing while you are mid-street, keep walking, because you will have time to finish crossing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-F09 | anchor: A02
A WALK signal or a green light means it is your turn to cross, not that it is safe; look first and cross only if it is safe. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-F10 | anchor: A03
The most common car-bicycle crashes happen when a driver turns left in front of an oncoming bicycle or turns right across a bicycle's path. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-F11 | anchor: A03
When turning left with a bicyclist coming from the opposite direction, wait for the rider to pass; when turning right with a bicyclist approaching on your right, let the rider through first. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-F12 | anchor: A03
On most roads bicyclists have the same rights and duties as other road users, but they are banned from limited-access highways, expressways and certain marked roads. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-F13 | anchor: A03
Bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road in the same direction as traffic, as far right as practical while avoiding hazards. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-F14 | anchor: A03
Tennessee law requires you to pass a bicycle going your way slowly and with at least 3 feet of clearance, keeping that space until you are safely past. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-F15 | anchor: A03
Never pass between a bicyclist and oncoming traffic on a two-lane road; slow down and wait until it is safe. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-F16 | anchor: A04
A marked and signed bicycle-only lane must never be used by drivers for turning, passing or parking. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec16-F17 | anchor: A04
Tennessee law requires a bicycle ridden at night to have a front lamp showing white light visible for at least 500 feet and a red reflector or red lamp visible from 500 feet behind. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec16-F18 | anchor: A05
Research shows two-thirds of car-motorcycle crashes are caused by the car driver turning in front of the motorcycle, often without ever seeing it. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-F19 | anchor: A05
Motorcycles are entitled to the full width of a lane, so never try to share a lane with one. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-F20 | anchor: A05
Pass a motorcycle as you would a car, but not too close or too fast, because the blast of air can push the rider out of control. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-F21 | anchor: A05
Allow at least a two-second following distance behind a motorcycle so the rider has time to maneuver or stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-F22 | anchor: A06
In crashes between cars and large trucks, the people in the car, usually the driver, suffer 78 percent of the deaths. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec16-F23 | anchor: A06
If you cannot see the truck driver in the truck's mirror, the truck driver cannot see you. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec16-F24 | anchor: A07
A loaded tractor-trailer may weigh up to 80,000 pounds, and a car at 55 mph can stop in about 240 feet while a truck at that speed needs about 450 feet or more. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-F25 | anchor: A07
Trucks must swing wide to the left to make a right turn, and they cannot see cars or motorcycles directly behind or beside them. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-F26 | anchor: A07
After passing a truck, do not move back in front of it until you can see the whole front of the truck in your rearview mirror, and do not slow down once you are ahead. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-F27 | anchor: A07
A truck's blind spots cover the area right in front of it, along both sides and up to 200 feet behind it. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-F28 | anchor: A07
On an uphill grade, keep to the left side of your lane while waiting behind a truck so its driver can see you, and leave extra room in case it rolls back. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-F29 | anchor: A08
When a truck passes you, keep to the far side of your lane and slow slightly, and never speed up while a truck or bus is passing. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-F30 | anchor: A08
Never cross behind a truck that is getting ready to back up, since you will be in the driver's blind spots. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-F31 | anchor: A08
If a truck going downhill has smoking wheels or is moving too fast, it may have lost its brakes, so fall back and do not pass. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-F32 | anchor: A09
Most children killed in school bus crashes are pedestrians aged five to seven, hit by the bus or by drivers illegally passing a stopped school bus. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec16-F33 | anchor: A09
Children are taught to stay ten feet from a school bus and take five giant steps away from it, so drivers must stop far enough back to leave that space. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec16-F34 | anchor: A09
Animal-drawn vehicles, most farm vehicles and construction equipment must display the slow-moving vehicle emblem, a fluorescent or reflective orange triangle, on the rear. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec16-F35 | anchor: A09
Farm machinery usually has no turn signals, may swing wide left before turning right, and usually travels under 25 mph. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec16-F36 | anchor: A09
When approaching or passing a horse being ridden or led along the road, use due care, keep a reasonable speed and distance, and do not honk or rev your engine. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec16-F37 | anchor: A10
In Tennessee, speeding in a reduced-speed work zone where transportation or construction workers are present brings a fine of up to $500. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec16-F38 | anchor: A10
Merge as soon as you learn a lane is closing ahead in a work zone; a last-chance merger can be ticketed and blamed for a crash. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec16-F39 | anchor: A11
Most work zone crashes are rear-end collisions, so do not tailgate and keep a safe distance from barriers, equipment and workers. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-F40 | anchor: A11
Drivers must always yield the right-of-way to trains, because a train cannot stop quickly; one going 55 mph needs a full mile to stop. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-F41 | anchor: A11
At a railroad crossing with electric or mechanical signals, a driver who must stop has to do so within 50 feet but no closer than 15 feet from the nearest rail. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-F42 | anchor: A11
Never drive around lowered crossing gates; stay stopped until the gates are fully up and the lights have stopped flashing. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-F43 | anchor: A12
If the lights start flashing or the gates begin to lower while you are already on the tracks, keep moving across and never back up. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec16-F44 | anchor: A12
If your vehicle stalls on the tracks, everyone should get out at once and move away from the tracks, even if no train is in sight, then call the number on the blue Emergency Notification System sign or 911. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec16-F45 | anchor: A12
If a train is coming toward your stalled vehicle, run toward the train at a 45-degree angle away from the tracks to avoid flying debris. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec16-F46 | anchor: A12
School buses, passenger buses and trucks carrying hazardous materials must stop at every railroad crossing, and you must never pass them there on a two-way road. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec16-F47 | anchor: A12
Tennessee law requires every occupant of a 15-passenger van to wear a safety belt at all times. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0128]

Misconceptions: an unmarked intersection still has a crosswalk; a green light or WALK signal does not mean it is safe to cross; a bicyclist away from the curb is not riding carelessly; a truck's high seat does not let its driver see everywhere; the wind between a passing truck and your car pushes you apart, not together; a driver stuck on the tracks when gates come down should keep going, not back up.
Mnemonics: left, right, left before crossing; three feet to pass a bike; see the truck's mirror or it cannot see you; orange means slow down; ten feet and five giant steps at the school bus.
Glossary: No-Zone means a blind-spot area around a truck or bus where crashes are more likely; right turn squeeze means getting trapped between a right-turning truck and the curb; slow-moving vehicle emblem means the orange triangle on slow farm and animal-drawn vehicles; Emergency Notification System sign means the blue railroad sign with a number to report stalled vehicles.
Dynamic facts: the bicycle passing distance, the work zone fine, the railroad stopping distances, the van belt law and the crash statistics in this chapter are set by Tennessee law or are dated figures; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.
